guide_what_is_json_s7_title: Working with JSON day to day
guide_what_is_json_s7_p1: Most developers meet JSON long before they read a spec for it. It shows up the first time you call an API and log the response, the first time you open a package.json, or the first time a colleague pastes a config snippet into chat. Getting comfortable reading it quickly pays off across almost every part of modern development.
guide_what_is_json_s7_p2: A few habits make that easier. Keep a formatter open so minified payloads become readable in one paste. Validate before you assume the data is wrong, since a single missing brace can look like a logic bug for an hour. And when a structure is deeply nested, a tree view saves you from counting brackets by hand.
guide_what_is_json_s7_p3: The format itself rarely changes, but the tooling around it keeps improving. Editors highlight it, browsers pretty print it in their dev tools, and databases now store and query it natively. Learning JSON well is one of those small investments that keeps paying off for years.
guide_what_is_json_faq_a4: Yes. Keys and string values are case sensitive, so "Name" and "name" are treated as two different keys. Most APIs settle on one convention, usually camelCase, and stick to it.
guide_what_is_json_faq_q5: Can a JSON file have more than one top-level value?
guide_what_is_json_faq_a5: No. A valid JSON document has exactly one root value, usually an object or an array. If you need to stream many records, a format like NDJSON puts one JSON value per line instead.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s6_p1: The honest answer is that the right format usually depends on who or what reads it next. If a browser or an API client is on the other end, JSON is almost always the path of least resistance. If a person edits the file by hand every week, the lighter syntax of YAML tends to win. XML earns its place where you need schemas, namespaces, or you are talking to a system that already speaks it.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s6_p2: You rarely have to commit to just one. Many teams keep configuration in YAML for readability, convert it to JSON at build time for their tooling, and send data as JSON over the wire. Converting between the three is cheap, so treat the choice as something you make per context rather than once for the whole project.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s6_p3: When in doubt, optimize for the reader who will be confused at 2am during an incident. Clear structure in a format their tools already understand beats a clever choice that saves a few characters.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_q3: Is JSON always smaller than XML?
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_a3: Almost always. JSON drops closing tags and most punctuation, so an equivalent document is typically 30 to 50 percent smaller than XML. YAML is usually close to JSON in size.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_q4: Can YAML do everything JSON can?
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_a4: YAML is a superset of JSON, so any valid JSON is also valid YAML. YAML adds features like comments and anchors that JSON does not have, which is part of why config files often prefer it.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s7_title: A quick checklist before you debug
guide_json_syntax_errors_s7_p1: When JSON refuses to parse, the cause is almost always mechanical rather than mysterious. Before you reach for a debugger, run through a short checklist. Are all keys and string values wrapped in double quotes rather than single ones? Is there a stray comma after the last item in an object or array? Does every opening brace and bracket have a matching close?
guide_json_syntax_errors_s7_p2: Two more issues catch most of the rest. Comments are not allowed in standard JSON, so a helpful note pasted from code will break the parse. And special characters inside strings, such as a literal newline or an unescaped backslash, need to be escaped. A formatter that validates as it goes will point at the exact line, which is faster than reading the whole file.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s7_p3: If the data comes from an API and still will not parse, check that you are looking at the response body and not the headers, and that it was not truncated in transit. Copying the raw payload into a validator removes any doubt about what the parser actually received.
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_q3: Why does my JSON work in JavaScript but fail in a strict parser?
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_a3: JavaScript object literals are more forgiving than JSON. They allow single quotes, unquoted keys, trailing commas, and comments. A strict JSON parser rejects all of those, which is why code that looks fine can still fail validation.
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_q4: What is the fastest way to find the exact error?
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_a4: Paste the text into a validating editor. It highlights the first line and column where parsing breaks, so instead of scanning the whole document you can jump straight to the problem.
guide_json_rest_api_s6_title: Designing JSON responses that age well
guide_json_rest_api_s6_p1: A REST response is a contract. Once clients depend on a field, removing or renaming it becomes a breaking change, so a little thought early saves a lot of migration later. Prefer clear, stable key names over clever abbreviations, and keep the same casing across every endpoint so consumers are not left guessing.
guide_json_rest_api_s6_p2: Wrapping data in a small envelope is a common pattern for a reason. A top-level object with a data field leaves room to add metadata such as pagination, timestamps, or a request id without disturbing the payload itself. Errors benefit from the same discipline: a consistent shape with a machine-readable code and a human-readable message lets clients handle failures without matching on strings.
guide_json_rest_api_s6_p3: Finally, be deliberate about null and missing fields. Returning null says the value is known to be empty, while omitting the key says nothing at all about it. Pick one meaning, document it, and apply it everywhere so clients can trust what they receive.
guide_json_rest_api_faq_q3: Should API responses be minified or formatted?
guide_json_rest_api_faq_a3: Send minified JSON over the wire to save bandwidth, since machines do not care about whitespace. Formatting is for humans, so pretty print only when you are reading or debugging a response.
guide_json_rest_api_faq_q4: What status code should go with a JSON error body?
guide_json_rest_api_faq_a4: Match the HTTP status to the situation, such as 400 for a bad request or 404 for a missing resource, and put the details in a consistent JSON error object. The status tells clients what happened, and the body explains why.
guide_json_schema_s6_p1: JSON Schema earns its keep at the boundaries of a system, where data you do not control arrives. Validating an incoming request, a config file, or a third-party webhook against a schema turns a vague runtime failure into a precise, early error that names the field at fault.
guide_json_schema_s6_p2: It also doubles as documentation that cannot drift. Because the schema is machine readable, the same file can validate data, generate example payloads, and drive editor autocomplete. Teams often keep the schema next to the code so a change to the data shape and a change to its rules travel together in the same review.
guide_json_schema_s6_p3: You do not need to describe everything at once. Start by requiring the handful of fields your code truly depends on, then tighten types and add constraints as the shape settles. A small schema that catches the common mistakes is more useful than an exhaustive one that never ships.
guide_json_schema_faq_q3: Is JSON Schema an official standard?
guide_json_schema_faq_a3: It is a widely adopted specification maintained as a set of IETF drafts, and most languages have mature validator libraries. Several drafts exist, so it helps to note which one your tools target.
guide_json_schema_faq_q4: Can I generate a schema from existing JSON?
guide_json_schema_faq_a4: Yes. Many tools infer a starting schema from a sample document, which you then refine by marking required fields and narrowing types. It is a fast way to get most of the way there.
guide_large_json_files_s7_p1: Large JSON becomes a problem in two different places: the program that has to hold it in memory, and the person who has to make sense of it. The two need different fixes, so it helps to know which one you are hitting before reaching for a tool.
guide_large_json_files_s7_p2: For raw size, streaming parsers read the file piece by piece instead of loading it all at once, which keeps memory flat even for files that would otherwise crash a tab. Newline-delimited JSON, where each line is its own record, makes this especially easy and lets you process a huge dataset one entry at a time. When you only need part of the data, filtering early beats loading everything and discarding most of it.
guide_large_json_files_s7_p3: For human readability, the trick is to avoid rendering the whole thing at once. A collapsible tree view lets you open only the branch you care about, and searching for a key is faster than scrolling. Because these tools run in your browser, even a large file never leaves your machine while you explore it.
guide_large_json_files_faq_q3: How large a JSON file can a browser handle?
guide_large_json_files_faq_a3: It depends on available memory rather than a fixed limit. Files up to a few hundred megabytes are usually fine on a modern machine, but rendering all of it at once is what tends to freeze a tab, not the parsing itself.
guide_large_json_files_faq_q4: What is NDJSON and when should I use it?
guide_large_json_files_faq_a4: NDJSON, or newline-delimited JSON, stores one JSON value per line. It is ideal for logs and large exports because you can read and process it one record at a time without loading the whole file into memory.

viewer_body1: Reading a large payload as text means holding the bracket nesting in your head while you scan. A tree does that for you: each object and array becomes a node you can collapse, so you can hide the ninety percent of the document you do not care about and look only at the branch you do. The raw editor stays alongside it, because sometimes you want to search the text.
viewer_body2: The tree also makes types explicit, which text does not. In raw JSON, 42 and "42" differ by two characters that are easy to skim past, and null, an empty string, and a missing key look similar enough to confuse when you are scanning quickly. Each node here carries its type, which turns a class of debugging question into something you can answer by looking.
formatter_body1: Formatting JSON is a parse and re-serialize round trip, not a text transformation. The input is parsed into values, then written back out with the indentation you chose. That distinction matters more than it sounds: anything that is not part of the parsed value cannot survive the trip, and anything the parser normalizes stays normalized in the output.
formatter_body2: The practical benefit is that formatting doubles as validation. A trailing comma, an unquoted key, or an unbalanced bracket fails at the parse step and is reported instead of silently producing broken output. When an API response will not load in your code, running it through the formatter is the fastest way to find out whether the payload itself is malformed or your parsing code is at fault.
minifier_body1: Minifying JSON removes the spaces, tabs, and line breaks that sit between tokens. Whitespace inside string values is untouched, because it is data rather than formatting. What is left is the shortest byte sequence that still parses to the same structure, which is what you want to store in a cache, put in a database column, or return from an endpoint.
minifier_body2: The size counter is the reason to use a minifier interactively rather than in a build step: it tells you whether the saving is worth anything for your particular payload. Deeply nested documents with short values benefit the most, because indentation is a large fraction of their bytes. Flat documents with long string values barely change at all.
sorter_body1: A canonical key order is worth having because JSON has no inherent one. Two services can emit the same data with keys in different sequences, and a text diff will call that a change. Sorting both sides first removes the disagreement, so what remains in the diff is a real difference in values.
sorter_body2: Sorting descends through objects and through the objects inside arrays, but never reorders array elements themselves. Array position usually carries meaning, so shuffling it would change the data rather than normalize it. The output is re-emitted with two space indentation, which also makes this a convenient way to normalize formatting and key order in one pass.
diff_body1: A text diff on JSON is noisy because it reacts to formatting, indentation, and key order, none of which are part of the data. This tool parses both sides first and then walks the two values together, so it reports differences in the structure rather than in the characters. Reformatting a file produces no output at all.
diff_body2: Every difference is reported as a path plus a marker: a plus for a key or index present only on the right, a minus for one present only on the left, and a tilde for a path that exists on both sides with different values. Paths use dots for object keys and square brackets for array indices, so you can paste one straight into your code to reach the value it names.
to_typescript_body1: The generator infers types from the values in your sample, which is the only information a single JSON document carries. There is no schema to read, so what you get out is a faithful description of what you put in, not a description of what the API can return. That distinction is the whole story of using generated types well.
to_typescript_body2: For an API you are integrating against, paste the fattest response you can find, ideally one where optional fields are populated and arrays are non empty. Then treat the output as a first draft: rename the root, widen fields you know can be absent, and replace inferred literals with the domain types you actually want. It saves the mechanical typing, not the thinking.
to_yaml_body1: YAML is a superset of JSON, so every JSON document has a YAML equivalent and the conversion never loses data. What it does change is how the values are written, and YAML has considerably more ways to write the same value than JSON does. Most of the interesting behaviour in this converter is about picking a form that reads back as the value you started with.
to_yaml_body2: The output uses two space indentation, a 120 character line width, and no reference aliases, which matches the conventions of Kubernetes manifests and the major CI configuration formats. Arrays are written as block sequences with a dash per element rather than inline, because that is what people expect to read and edit in a config file.
to_csv_body1: CSV is a flat, rectangular format and JSON is a nested, ragged one, so this conversion is genuinely lossy in shape even when no value is lost. Every record has to occupy one row with the same columns as every other record, which means the converter has to decide what to do about keys that only some records have and values that are not scalars.
to_csv_body2: The answers here are the pragmatic ones. The header row is the union of every key seen across every record, in the order the keys were first encountered. A record missing one of those keys gets an empty cell. A value that is itself an object or an array is written into the cell as JSON text. Nothing is dropped, but a nested structure arrives in the spreadsheet as a string rather than as columns.
csv_to_json_body1: Reading CSV is harder than it looks, because the format is a family of conventions rather than a single specification. This parser scans the whole document rather than splitting it into lines first, which is what lets a newline inside a quoted field stay part of that field instead of tearing the record in half. Line feed, carriage return, and the pair of them are all accepted as record separators, so files from Windows tools work without conversion.
csv_to_json_body2: Doubled double quotes inside a quoted field are read as one literal quote, blank lines are skipped rather than becoming rows of empty strings, and a record with fewer fields than the header gets empty strings for the remainder. What the parser deliberately does not do is guess types, which is the subject of the section below.
to_xml_body1: JSON and XML describe overlapping but not identical things, so this conversion involves real decisions rather than a mechanical substitution. XML has attributes, namespaces, comments, processing instructions, and mixed content, none of which JSON has. JSON has arrays and a distinction between a number and a string, neither of which XML has. Every JSON to XML converter picks a convention, and knowing which one you are using is the difference between output that works and output that almost works.
to_xml_body2: The convention here is the simplest defensible one. Every key becomes an element, never an attribute. Array items repeat the element name of the key that held them. A null value and an empty object both become a self closing element. The document is wrapped in a single root element and prefixed with an XML declaration, so what you copy out is a complete, parseable document rather than a fragment.

viewer_faq_a1: No. PureJSON processes everything 100% client-side using your browser. No data is ever transmitted to any server.

formatter_faq_q2: Does formatting change my JSON data?

minifier_faq_q1: How much space can I save by minifying?
minifier_faq_a1: Between roughly 20 and 60 percent of raw bytes, depending on how deeply nested the document is and how short its values are. On a measured 40 record sample it was 41.7 percent. Over HTTP with gzip enabled the real saving drops to around 10 percent.
minifier_faq_q2: Does minifying change my JSON data?
minifier_faq_a2: No. Minification only removes whitespace. Your data values remain exactly the same.
minifier_faq_q3: Can I minify already minified JSON?
minifier_faq_a3: Yes, but there will be no size reduction since the JSON is already compact. The output will be identical to the input.
minifier_faq_a4: No. Minified JSON is fully valid JSON. It is simply more compact and harder for humans to read, but perfectly parseable by any JSON parser.
minifier_faq_q5: Should I minify JSON that my server already gzips?
minifier_faq_a5: Usually not worth a build step. Gzip removes repeated whitespace very efficiently, so on a measured sample minification only cut a further 10.3 percent after compression. Minify when bytes are counted uncompressed, such as in a database column or localStorage.

to_typescript_faq_a1: They accurately describe the sample you pasted. Whether that matches the API contract depends on how representative your sample is. Paste an array of several records with optional fields both present and absent for the best result.
to_typescript_faq_q2: Can I customize the generated interface names?
to_typescript_faq_a2: The root interface is named RootObject. Rename it after copying into your project, along with any nested interface names you want to change.
to_typescript_faq_a3: Yes. Each nested object gets its own interface, and the parent interface references it by name. Deeply nested structures are fully supported.
to_typescript_faq_q4: What about arrays with mixed types?
to_typescript_faq_a4: They become a union of the observed element types. An array holding strings and numbers is typed (string | number)[]. An empty array becomes any[], because there is nothing to infer an element type from.
to_typescript_faq_q5: Why is my field typed null instead of optional?
to_typescript_faq_a5: A null value only tells the generator that null occurred, not what the field holds when it is populated. You get the type null, which you should widen by hand to something like string | null. Optionality is a separate signal and comes only from keys missing across array elements.

to_yaml_usecase2: Transforming JSON settings into YAML for CI/CD pipeline configuration (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI)
to_yaml_usecase3: Creating YAML-based configuration files from JSON templates
to_yaml_faq_a1: Yes. The converter produces valid YAML that can be used directly in configuration files, Kubernetes manifests, and other YAML-compatible tools.
to_yaml_faq_q2: Does YAML support all JSON data types?
to_yaml_faq_a2: Yes. YAML is a superset of JSON, so all JSON data types (strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, objects) are fully supported.
to_yaml_faq_a3: JSON has no comment syntax, so a JSON input never carries comments to preserve. If your data originally came from a commented YAML file, those comments were lost when it was converted to JSON, before reaching this tool.
to_yaml_faq_q4: Can I convert YAML back to JSON?
to_yaml_faq_a4: Not with this tool directly. PureJSON focuses on JSON-to-YAML conversion. However, since YAML is a superset of JSON, you can use a YAML parser to convert back.
to_yaml_faq_q5: How does it handle values like no and yes?
to_yaml_faq_a5: Yes, and more carefully than you might expect. Values that a YAML 1.1 reader could coerce into a boolean or a number are quoted automatically. The strings "yes", "no", and "1.10" all come out quoted so they read back as strings.

to_csv_faq_q1: What JSON structure works best for CSV?
to_csv_faq_a1: An array of objects with consistent keys works best. Each object becomes a row, and each key becomes a column header.
to_csv_faq_a2: They are serialized as JSON text inside a single cell, then quoted because that text contains double quotes. They are not expanded into separate columns.
to_csv_faq_q3: What if objects have different keys?
to_csv_faq_a3: The header row is the union of every key found across all records, ordered by when each key was first seen. A record that lacks one of those keys gets an empty cell for it.
to_csv_faq_q4: Can I convert a single JSON object (not an array)?
to_csv_faq_a4: Yes. A single object is treated as a one-row table, with keys as headers and values as the single data row.
to_csv_faq_q5: Are nested objects flattened into separate columns?
to_csv_faq_a5: No. A nested object arrives in one cell as JSON text. Flatten the structure in your own code first if you want each nested field as its own column.
csv_to_json_description: Convert CSV data to JSON format online. Transform spreadsheet data into structured JSON arrays.
csv_to_json_intro: Turn a spreadsheet export into an array of objects. The header row supplies the keys, and quoted fields containing commas or line breaks are parsed correctly.
csv_to_json_howto_s1_desc: Paste a spreadsheet export or database dump whose first line names the columns.
csv_to_json_howto_s2_desc: Each subsequent row is converted to a JSON object using the header values as keys.
csv_to_json_howto_s3_desc: Copy the JSON array output for use in your application, API, or database.
csv_to_json_feature1: Automatic header detection from the first row
csv_to_json_feature2: Proper parsing of quoted fields with commas and newlines
csv_to_json_feature3: Handles escaped double quotes within fields
csv_to_json_feature4: Clean, formatted JSON output with 2-space indentation
csv_to_json_usecase1: Importing spreadsheet data into a web application or API
csv_to_json_usecase2: Converting CSV exports from databases into JSON for frontend use
csv_to_json_usecase3: Transforming CSV log files into structured JSON for analysis
csv_to_json_faq_q1: Does the CSV need a header row?
csv_to_json_faq_a1: Yes. The first row is treated as column headers and used as JSON object keys.
csv_to_json_faq_a2: Yes. Fields enclosed in double quotes are parsed correctly, including fields containing commas, line breaks, and doubled double quotes as escaped quotes.
csv_to_json_faq_q3: Are all values treated as strings?
csv_to_json_faq_a3: Yes, every value is emitted as a string. CSV carries no type information, and guessing would turn a postal code like 07030 into 7030 and a part number like 1E5 into 100000. Convert the columns you know are numeric in your own code.
csv_to_json_faq_a4: The comma only. Tab and semicolon separated files are not parsed, which matters for exports from spreadsheets in locales that use the comma as a decimal separator. Re-export as comma separated first.
csv_to_json_faq_q5: Can I convert CSV without a header row?
csv_to_json_faq_a5: The first row is always treated as the header. If your CSV has no header, add column names as the first row before converting.
to_xml_description: Convert JSON to XML format online. Transform your JSON data into well-formed XML documents.
to_xml_intro: Convert JSON into a well formed XML document for SOAP endpoints, legacy integrations, and tools that still expect angle brackets. Keys become elements and array items become repeated siblings.
to_xml_howto_s1_desc: Paste the JSON you need to hand to an XML consumer, such as a SOAP request body.
to_xml_howto_s2_desc: The tool generates well-formed XML with proper indentation and an XML declaration.
to_xml_howto_s3_desc: Copy the XML output for use in SOAP services, legacy systems, or XML-based configurations.
to_xml_feature1: Includes XML declaration with UTF-8 encoding
to_xml_feature3: Nested objects and arrays are converted to nested XML elements
to_xml_feature4: Clean indentation for readable XML output
to_xml_usecase1: Integrating JSON data with SOAP or XML-based web services
to_xml_usecase2: Converting JSON configuration to XML format for legacy systems
to_xml_usecase3: Generating XML documents from JSON data for data exchange
to_xml_faq_a1: Yes. The output has an XML declaration, exactly one root element, escaped special characters, and element names that satisfy the XML naming rules, including keys that start with a digit and top level arrays.
to_xml_faq_q2: How are arrays converted to XML?
to_xml_faq_a2: Array items repeat the element name of the key that held them, producing sibling elements. A top level array is the exception: it is wrapped in a single root element with each entry written as an item element, because XML permits only one root.
to_xml_faq_q3: What about JSON keys with special characters?
to_xml_faq_a3: Characters that XML does not allow in a name are replaced with underscores. A name that would begin with a digit or a hyphen also gets an underscore prefix, so the key 2nd becomes the element _2nd rather than invalid markup.
to_xml_faq_a4: Currently, the root element is named 'root' by default. You can rename it in the output after copying.
to_xml_faq_q5: Does the converter support XML attributes?
to_xml_faq_a5: JSON keys are converted to XML elements, not attributes. If you need attributes, you can manually edit the XML output after conversion.
sorter_description: Sort JSON object keys alphabetically. Organize your JSON data for better readability and consistency.
sorter_intro: Reorder every object key in a document so two files line up and version control diffs stop reporting noise. Nested objects are sorted at every level and array order is left alone.
sorter_howto_s1_desc: Drop in a config file or a payload whose keys arrive in an unpredictable order.
sorter_howto_s2_desc: Select ascending (A→Z) or descending (Z→A) from the dropdown.
sorter_howto_s3_desc: All object keys are sorted recursively, including nested objects. Arrays remain in their original order.
sorter_feature1: Recursive sorting: all nested object keys are sorted at every level
sorter_feature3: Preserves array element order: only object keys are reordered
sorter_usecase1: Standardizing JSON key order for consistent version control diffs
sorter_usecase2: Organizing configuration files for better readability
sorter_usecase3: Preparing JSON for comparison: sorting both files before diffing reduces noise
sorter_faq_a1: Yes, at every level. Objects nested inside other objects and objects nested inside arrays are all sorted, independently of their parent.
sorter_faq_a2: No. Only object keys are sorted. Array element order is preserved.
sorter_faq_a3: No. Only the order of object keys is changed. All values, arrays, and nested structures remain identical.
sorter_faq_a4: Sorted keys make JSON easier to read and compare. They also reduce diff noise in version control, since key order changes won't appear as modifications.
sorter_faq_q5: Is the sort alphabetical or by character code?
sorter_faq_a5: Keys are compared using browser locale collation, so letters take priority over case and accents fold to their base letter. Feeding in Beta, alpha, Alpha returns alpha, Alpha, Beta, which is different from a code point sort.
diff_description: Compare two JSON documents and find differences. Highlight added, removed, and changed values.
diff_intro: Compare two JSON documents structurally instead of as text. Each difference is reported with the exact path where it occurs, so you can see what changed without reading both files.
diff_howto_s1_desc: Put the version you are treating as the baseline on the left, such as the current production response.
diff_howto_s2_desc: Paste the modified JSON document into the right panel.
diff_howto_s3_desc: The tool compares both documents recursively and shows all differences with their JSON paths.
diff_feature1: Deep recursive comparison of nested objects and arrays
diff_feature2: Path-based output showing exact location of each difference
diff_feature3: Three change types: added (+), removed (-), and changed (~)
diff_feature4: Load JSON from files for easy comparison of large documents
diff_usecase1: Comparing API responses before and after a code change
diff_usecase2: Reviewing configuration file changes between environments (dev, staging, production)
diff_usecase3: Validating data migration results by comparing source and target records
diff_faq_a1: Each difference shows the JSON path, type of change (added, removed, or changed), and the old/new values.
diff_faq_a2: Yes. The comparison is recursive and detects differences at every nesting level, including arrays.
diff_faq_a3: By index. Element zero is compared with element zero, and so on. Elements beyond the length of the shorter array are reported as added or removed at their index. Moved elements are not detected as moves.
diff_faq_q4: What if both JSONs are identical?
diff_faq_a4: If no differences are found, the result will display 'No differences found.' confirming that both documents are identical.
diff_faq_q5: Can I compare very large JSON files?
diff_faq_a5: Yes, but performance depends on your browser. For very large files (over 10 MB), the comparison may take a few seconds. All processing happens locally.

guide_what_is_json_title: What is JSON? A Complete Beginner's Guide: PureJSON
guide_what_is_json_description: Learn what JSON is, how it works, and why it's the most popular data format for web development. Includes examples and practical tips.
guide_what_is_json_h1: What is JSON? A Complete Beginner's Guide
guide_what_is_json_intro: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight, text-based data interchange format that has become the standard for transmitting data between web applications and servers. Despite its name, JSON is language-independent and is supported by virtually every modern programming language.
guide_what_is_json_s1_p1: At its core, JSON is built on two universal data structures: objects (collections of key-value pairs) and arrays (ordered lists of values). These simple building blocks can represent complex, nested data structures that are easy for both humans to read and machines to parse.
guide_what_is_json_s1_p2: A JSON object is enclosed in curly braces {} and contains key-value pairs separated by commas. Keys must be strings wrapped in double quotes, and values can be strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, or other objects.
guide_what_is_json_s2_p1: JSON supports six data types that cover most data representation needs. Understanding these types is essential for working with JSON effectively.
guide_what_is_json_s2_li1: String: Text enclosed in double quotes: "hello world"
guide_what_is_json_s3_p1: Before JSON, XML was the dominant data interchange format. However, JSON's simplicity and smaller file size made it a natural fit for web APIs. A typical JSON response is 30-50% smaller than an equivalent XML response, which means faster data transfer and lower bandwidth costs.
guide_what_is_json_s3_p2: JSON's native compatibility with JavaScript gave it an early advantage in web development, but its true strength lies in universal support. Whether you're working in Python, Java, Go, Rust, or any other modern language, JSON parsing libraries are readily available and well-optimized.
guide_what_is_json_s3_p3: Today, JSON is used everywhere: REST APIs, configuration files (like package.json and tsconfig.json), NoSQL databases (MongoDB, CouchDB), and even communication protocols like JSON-RPC.
guide_what_is_json_s4_p1: JSON is incredibly versatile. Here are the most common scenarios where you'll encounter JSON in real-world development:
guide_what_is_json_s4_li1: API Communication: REST APIs almost universally use JSON for request and response bodies
guide_what_is_json_s4_li2: Configuration Files: Tools like npm, TypeScript, ESLint, and VS Code use JSON for settings
guide_what_is_json_s4_li3: Data Storage: NoSQL databases like MongoDB store documents in JSON-like formats (BSON)
guide_what_is_json_s4_li4: Data Exchange: Sharing structured data between different systems and programming languages
guide_what_is_json_s4_li5: Logging: Structured logging in JSON format makes logs searchable and parseable
guide_what_is_json_s5_p1: When working with JSON data, you'll frequently need to format, validate, and transform it. Raw JSON from APIs often comes minified (without whitespace), making it difficult to read. A JSON formatter adds proper indentation so you can quickly understand the data structure.
guide_what_is_json_s5_p2: For debugging API responses, a JSON viewer with tree navigation helps you explore deeply nested structures without getting lost. You can expand and collapse sections to focus on the data you need.
guide_what_is_json_s5_p3: If you need to convert JSON to other formats for different tools or team members, PureJSON offers converters for YAML, CSV, XML, and TypeScript interfaces: all running locally in your browser with no data sent to any server.
guide_what_is_json_s6_p1: Follow these guidelines to write clean, maintainable JSON:
guide_what_is_json_s6_li1: Always use double quotes for keys and string values: single quotes are not valid JSON
guide_what_is_json_s6_li2: Avoid trailing commas: the last item in an object or array must not have a comma after it
guide_what_is_json_s6_li3: Use consistent naming conventions: camelCase is most common in JSON APIs
guide_what_is_json_s6_li4: Keep nesting levels reasonable: deeply nested JSON is hard to read and work with
guide_what_is_json_s6_li5: Use meaningful key names: "userName" is better than "un"
guide_what_is_json_faq_q1: Is JSON the same as JavaScript?
guide_what_is_json_faq_a1: No. JSON is a data format inspired by JavaScript object syntax, but it is language-independent. JSON has stricter rules than JavaScript: for example, keys must be in double quotes and trailing commas are not allowed.
guide_what_is_json_faq_a2: No. Standard JSON does not support comments. If you need comments in configuration files, consider using JSONC (JSON with Comments) or YAML instead. Some tools like VS Code support JSONC for their config files.
guide_what_is_json_faq_q3: What's the maximum size of a JSON file?
guide_what_is_json_faq_a3: JSON itself has no size limit. Practical limits depend on the parser and available memory. Most web APIs limit request/response sizes to a few megabytes, while file-based JSON can be much larger.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_title: JSON vs YAML vs XML: When to Use Which: PureJSON
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_description: Compare JSON, YAML, and XML data formats. Learn the strengths, weaknesses, and best use cases for each format.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_h1: JSON vs YAML vs XML: When to Use Which
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_intro: Choosing the right data format can significantly impact developer productivity and application performance. JSON, YAML, and XML are the three most widely used structured data formats, each with distinct strengths. This guide helps you make an informed choice for your specific use case.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s1_p1: All three formats can represent hierarchical, structured data, but they differ in syntax, readability, features, and ecosystem support. Here's a high-level comparison:
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s1_li1: JSON: Lightweight, fast parsing, native JavaScript support, widely used in web APIs
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s1_li2: YAML: Human-readable, supports comments, popular for configuration files (Kubernetes, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions)
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s1_li3: XML: Feature-rich (attributes, namespaces, schemas), dominant in enterprise systems and SOAP APIs
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s2_p1: JSON's strength lies in its simplicity and universal support. Every major programming language has built-in or standard library JSON support. It's the default format for REST APIs, making it the most common choice for web development.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s2_p2: JSON's main limitations are the lack of comments (making it less ideal for configuration files that need documentation) and no built-in schema system (though JSON Schema exists as a separate specification).
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s3_p1: YAML uses indentation instead of braces, making it visually cleaner and easier to read for configuration files. It supports comments with #, which is essential for documenting configuration choices.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s3_p2: However, YAML's whitespace sensitivity can cause subtle bugs: a wrong indent can completely change the meaning of your data. This makes YAML more error-prone than JSON for machine-generated content.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s4_p1: XML remains essential in enterprise environments, especially for SOAP web services, document formats (HTML, SVG, RSS), and systems that require strict data validation through DTD or XML Schema (XSD).
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s4_p2: XML's verbosity is its biggest drawback: tags add significant overhead compared to JSON. An XML document is typically 2-3x larger than the equivalent JSON, impacting transfer speed and storage.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s5_p1: Choose the format based on your primary need:
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s5_li1: Use JSON for: REST APIs, web applications, data interchange between services, NoSQL databases
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s5_li2: Use YAML for: Configuration files, CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose files
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s5_li3: Use XML for: SOAP APIs, document markup, enterprise integrations, systems requiring strict schemas
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_s5_p2: Need to convert between formats? PureJSON can convert JSON to YAML and JSON to XML instantly in your browser.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_q1: Is YAML a superset of JSON?
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_a1: Yes. Valid JSON is also valid YAML (in YAML 1.2). This means you can use a YAML parser to read JSON files, but not the other way around.
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_q2: Which format is fastest to parse?
guide_json_vs_yaml_xml_faq_a2: JSON is typically the fastest to parse because of its simple syntax and widespread optimization. YAML parsers are generally slower due to the complex grammar. XML parsing speed varies but is usually between JSON and YAML.
guide_json_syntax_errors_title: Common JSON Syntax Errors and How to Fix Them: PureJSON
guide_json_syntax_errors_description: Learn to identify and fix the most common JSON syntax errors. Practical examples and solutions for every JSON mistake.
guide_json_syntax_errors_h1: Common JSON Syntax Errors and How to Fix Them
guide_json_syntax_errors_intro: JSON's strict syntax rules mean that even a small mistake will cause a parsing error. Unlike JavaScript, JSON has no tolerance for trailing commas, single quotes, or unquoted keys. This guide covers the most frequent errors developers encounter and how to fix each one.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s1_p1: The most common JSON error is a trailing comma after the last item in an object or array. JavaScript allows this, but JSON does not.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s2_title: Single Quotes Instead of Double Quotes
guide_json_syntax_errors_s2_p1: JSON requires double quotes for all strings and keys. Single quotes, backticks, or unquoted keys are not valid.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s3_p1: Standard JSON does not support any form of comments. If you paste JSON that contains // or /* */ comments, the parser will fail. Remove all comments before parsing, or use a JSONC-aware parser.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s4_p1: In JavaScript objects, keys without special characters don't need quotes. In JSON, every key must be a double-quoted string: no exceptions.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s5_p1: JSON only supports specific value types. Common mistakes include using undefined, NaN, Infinity, or functions: none of which are valid in JSON.
guide_json_syntax_errors_s6_p1: When you encounter a JSON parsing error, try these steps:
guide_json_syntax_errors_s6_li1: Paste your JSON into the JSON Formatter: it will show the exact error location
guide_json_syntax_errors_s6_li2: Check for trailing commas, especially after copy-pasting from code
guide_json_syntax_errors_s6_li3: Verify all strings use double quotes, not single quotes or backticks
guide_json_syntax_errors_s6_li5: Ensure all values are valid JSON types (no undefined, NaN, or functions)
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_a1: Douglas Crockford, who specified JSON, deliberately omitted comments to keep the format simple and to prevent abuse of comments for parsing directives. For files that need comments, consider YAML or JSONC.
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_q2: Can I validate JSON without a tool?
guide_json_syntax_errors_faq_a2: You can use JSON.parse() in any browser's developer console. If it throws a SyntaxError, the JSON is invalid. The error message will often indicate the position of the problem.
guide_json_rest_api_title: How to Use JSON in REST APIs: PureJSON
guide_json_rest_api_description: Learn how JSON works with REST APIs. Understand request/response formats, headers, status codes, and best practices for API development.
guide_json_rest_api_h1: How to Use JSON in REST APIs
guide_json_rest_api_intro: JSON is the lingua franca of REST APIs. Nearly every modern web API sends and receives data in JSON format. This guide explains how JSON fits into the REST architecture, covering headers, request bodies, response structures, and practical tips for working with API data.
guide_json_rest_api_s1_p1: When sending data to an API (POST, PUT, PATCH requests), you include JSON in the request body and set the Content-Type header to application/json. This tells the server how to parse the incoming data.
guide_json_rest_api_s2_p1: API responses typically include JSON in the body with a Content-Type: application/json header. The response structure usually follows conventions like wrapping data in a top-level object with metadata.
guide_json_rest_api_s3_p1: Well-designed APIs follow consistent JSON response patterns. Here are the most common structures you'll encounter:
guide_json_rest_api_s4_p1: API responses often come minified (no whitespace) to save bandwidth. To read them, paste the response into PureJSON's JSON Viewer to get a formatted, navigable tree view. For TypeScript projects, use the JSON to TypeScript converter to generate type definitions from sample API responses.
guide_json_rest_api_s4_p2: When comparing API responses between environments (staging vs production) or before/after a code change, the JSON Diff tool highlights exactly what changed.
guide_json_rest_api_s5_p1: Follow these conventions when designing or consuming JSON APIs:
guide_json_rest_api_s5_li1: Use camelCase for JSON property names (most common convention)
guide_json_rest_api_s5_li4: Return consistent error responses with meaningful error codes and messages
guide_json_rest_api_s5_li5: Use pagination for large collections to avoid sending too much data at once
guide_json_rest_api_faq_q1: Why do APIs use JSON instead of XML?
guide_json_rest_api_faq_a1: JSON is smaller, faster to parse, and natively supported in JavaScript. Most modern APIs chose JSON for better performance and simpler integration with web frontends.
guide_json_rest_api_faq_q2: Should I always use application/json content type?
guide_json_rest_api_faq_a2: For JSON data, yes. Some APIs also accept text/json, but application/json is the standard MIME type. For file uploads, use multipart/form-data instead.
guide_json_schema_title: JSON Schema: Validate Your Data Structure: PureJSON
guide_json_schema_description: Learn JSON Schema for data validation. Understand types, required fields, patterns, and how to ensure your JSON data is always correct.
guide_json_schema_h1: JSON Schema: Validate Your Data Structure
guide_json_schema_intro: JSON Schema is a vocabulary that lets you annotate and validate JSON documents. It defines the expected structure, data types, and constraints for your JSON data. Think of it as TypeScript types, but for any JSON data: not just JavaScript objects.
guide_json_schema_s1_p1: JSON Schema is itself written in JSON. It describes what valid data looks like: which properties are required, what types they should be, value ranges, string patterns, and more. Validators use the schema to check whether a JSON document conforms to the expected structure.
guide_json_schema_s2_p1: JSON Schema uses keywords to define constraints. Here are the most commonly used ones:
guide_json_schema_s2_li2: required: Array of property names that must be present
guide_json_schema_s2_li3: properties: Defines the schema for each property of an object
guide_json_schema_s2_li4: items: Defines the schema for array elements
guide_json_schema_s2_li5: enum: Restricts a value to a fixed set of options
guide_json_schema_s2_li6: pattern: Validates a string against a regular expression
guide_json_schema_s3_p1: Here's a realistic JSON Schema for validating user registration data. It ensures the username is between 3-20 characters, the email is valid, the password meets minimum length requirements, and the age is within a reasonable range.
guide_json_schema_s4_p1: JSON Schema is used across the development stack for data validation:
guide_json_schema_s4_li1: API Validation: Validate request bodies before processing (Express, FastAPI, Spring Boot)
guide_json_schema_s4_li2: Form Validation: Generate forms from schemas and validate input client-side
guide_json_schema_s4_li3: Documentation: OpenAPI (Swagger) uses JSON Schema to describe API data models
guide_json_schema_s4_li4: Configuration: VS Code uses JSON Schema to provide autocomplete for settings.json
guide_json_schema_s4_li5: Testing: Validate API responses against expected schemas in integration tests
guide_json_schema_s5_p1: If you work with TypeScript, you might wonder why you need JSON Schema when you already have type checking. The key difference is that TypeScript types only exist at compile time: they're erased when your code runs. JSON Schema validates data at runtime, which is essential for external data (API inputs, file uploads, user input).
guide_json_schema_s5_p2: You can use PureJSON's JSON to TypeScript converter to generate TypeScript interfaces from your data, and JSON Schema for runtime validation: they complement each other.
guide_json_schema_faq_q1: Is JSON Schema hard to learn?
guide_json_schema_faq_a1: The basics are straightforward: you can start validating data with just type, required, and properties. Advanced features like conditional schemas and references take more time but aren't needed for most use cases.
guide_json_schema_faq_q2: What tools validate JSON against a schema?
guide_json_schema_faq_a2: Popular validators include Ajv (JavaScript), jsonschema (Python), and everit-org/json-schema (Java). Most web frameworks have built-in or plugin-based JSON Schema validation support.
guide_large_json_files_title: Working with Large JSON Files: Tips and Best Practices: PureJSON
guide_large_json_files_description: Learn strategies for handling large JSON files efficiently. Tips for performance, memory management, and practical tools.
guide_large_json_files_h1: Working with Large JSON Files: Tips and Best Practices
guide_large_json_files_intro: As applications grow, so does the JSON data they produce. API exports, log files, and database dumps can easily reach hundreds of megabytes. Standard tools and approaches that work for small JSON files break down at scale. This guide covers practical strategies for working with large JSON files efficiently.
guide_large_json_files_s1_title: Why Large JSON Files Are Challenging
guide_large_json_files_s1_p1: Most JSON parsers load the entire document into memory at once. A 500 MB JSON file can easily consume 2-4 GB of RAM when parsed into objects due to memory overhead from data structures, pointers, and string representations.
guide_large_json_files_s1_p2: Browser-based tools face additional limits: most browsers cap individual tab memory at 1-4 GB. This means a JSON file larger than about 100 MB may cause browser tabs to crash when loaded into a standard JSON viewer.
guide_large_json_files_s2_p1: If you're sharing or uploading JSON files, minify them first. Removing whitespace and indentation typically reduces file size by 20-60%, depending on the original formatting. This saves bandwidth and upload time with no data loss.
guide_large_json_files_s3_p1: For files too large to load into memory, use streaming JSON parsers. These process the file token by token without building the entire tree in memory:
guide_large_json_files_s3_li1: JavaScript/Node.js: Use JSONStream or stream-json packages for streaming parse
guide_large_json_files_s3_li3: Command line: Use jq for filtering and transforming large JSON from the terminal
guide_large_json_files_s4_p1: If your large JSON file is an array of objects (common for exports and logs), split it into smaller chunks. Process each chunk separately, then combine results. Many command-line tools like jq and split can help with this approach.
guide_large_json_files_s4_p2: For structured analysis, consider converting your JSON array to CSV format, which can be opened in spreadsheet tools or loaded into databases for querying.
guide_large_json_files_s5_p1: JSON isn't always the best format for very large datasets. Consider these alternatives for specific scenarios:
guide_large_json_files_s5_li1: NDJSON (Newline Delimited JSON): One JSON object per line, ideal for logs and streaming
guide_large_json_files_s5_li2: CSV: More compact for tabular data, supported by all spreadsheet tools
guide_large_json_files_s5_li3: Parquet/Avro: Binary formats optimized for large dataset analytics
guide_large_json_files_s5_li4: SQLite: Queryable database in a single file, great for structured data
guide_large_json_files_s6_p1: PureJSON runs entirely in your browser, so performance depends on your device. For optimal results with larger files:
guide_large_json_files_s6_li1: Files under 5 MB: All tools work smoothly
guide_large_json_files_s6_li2: Files 5-50 MB: Formatting and minification work well; tree view may be slow
guide_large_json_files_s6_li3: Files 50+ MB: Consider using command-line tools like jq instead
guide_large_json_files_s6_li4: Use JSON Formatter to format and quickly skim structure, then extract sections of interest
guide_large_json_files_faq_q1: What's the largest JSON file I can open in PureJSON?
guide_large_json_files_faq_a1: It depends on your browser and device memory. Most modern browsers handle files up to 50 MB without issues. For larger files, use command-line tools like jq.
guide_large_json_files_faq_q2: Does minification really help with large files?
guide_large_json_files_faq_a2: Yes. A 100 MB formatted JSON file with 4-space indentation typically becomes 40-60 MB after minification. This saves significant time for transfers, storage, and API responses.

formatter_deep_p1: Indentation is the only thing you asked to change, but a parse and re-serialize cycle normalizes numbers as a side effect. JSON has one numeric type and JavaScript reads it as a double, so the written form of a number is regenerated from its value rather than copied. The literal 1.0 comes back as 1, 1e3 becomes 1000, and 0.10 becomes 0.1. The numeric value is identical in every case, but the text is not byte for byte what you pasted.
formatter_deep_p2: Integers larger than 2 to the 53rd power cannot be held exactly in a double, so they are the one case where formatting genuinely loses information. Paste 12345678901234567890 and the output reads 12345678901234567000. If your payload carries large IDs, snowflake identifiers, or currency values as bare numbers, treat any JSON tool that round trips through a native parser as unsafe for those fields, this one included. Sending such IDs as strings is the usual fix, and it is worth doing at the API level.
formatter_deep_p3: Key order is preserved for ordinary keys, because objects keep insertion order. Keys that look like array indices are the exception: integer-like keys are always visited in ascending numeric order and placed ahead of every string key. An object written as 10, 2, b, a comes back as 2, 10, b, a. This is a property of the object model underneath, not a choice the formatter makes, and every browser based JSON tool behaves the same way.
formatter_ref_intro: Each row is a real input and the exact output this tool produces. Only the last two rows change anything you would notice in your data.
formatter_ref_n1: Trailing zeros are dropped. The value is unchanged.
formatter_ref_n2: Exponent notation is expanded when the plain form is shorter.
formatter_ref_n3: A leading zero is kept, a trailing one is not.
formatter_ref_n4: Duplicate keys are legal to parse but only the last one survives. Nothing warns you.
formatter_ref_n5: Integer-like keys sort numerically and move ahead of string keys.
formatter_ref_n6: Beyond 2^53 the value itself changes. This is the one lossy case.
formatter_ex_intro: A typical minified API payload, formatted with two space indentation.
formatter_ex_note: Notice that the nested object and the array each gain one indentation level, and that array elements sit on their own lines. The values are untouched.
formatter_pit1_t: Tab indentation is not the same as one space
formatter_pit1_d: A common bug in JSON formatters is passing the number 1 when the user asks for tabs, because the serializer treats a number as a space count. The result is one space per level, not a tab. This tool passes an actual tab character, so the Tab setting produces tab indented output that your editor will show at your configured tab width.
formatter_pit2_t: Formatting cannot fix JSON with comments or trailing commas
formatter_pit2_d: Comments and trailing commas belong to JSON5 and JSONC, not to JSON. The parse step rejects them, so you get an error rather than cleaned up output. If you are formatting a tsconfig.json or a VS Code settings file, strip the comments first or use a JSONC aware tool.
formatter_pit3_t: Do not use formatting to canonicalize for signature checks
formatter_pit3_d: Because numbers are normalized and duplicate keys collapse, formatted output is not a canonical form you can hash and compare against a signature produced elsewhere. Use a canonicalization scheme such as JCS if you need byte stable output across implementations.
formatter_faq_q6: Why did my large ID number change?
formatter_faq_a6: JSON numbers are read as double precision floats, which hold integers exactly only up to 2^53. A 20 digit ID gets rounded during parsing, before formatting even happens. Ask the API to send such IDs as JSON strings, which is the standard workaround.
formatter_faq_q7: Does formatting preserve the order of my keys?
formatter_faq_a7: Ordinary keys keep their original order. Keys that consist only of digits are an exception: they are emitted in ascending numeric order and placed before all other keys, because that is how the underlying object model stores them.
minifier_deep_title: How much minification really saves once gzip is involved
minifier_deep_p1: Raw minification numbers look impressive and are usually quoted on their own, which is misleading for anything served over HTTP. Almost every server and CDN already applies gzip or brotli, and compressors are extremely good at repeated whitespace. Indentation is the most repetitive content in a pretty printed document, so it is precisely what gzip eliminates for free.
minifier_deep_p2: Here is a measurement on a 40 record array of user objects, the shape of a typical list endpoint response. Pretty printed with two space indentation it is 10,562 bytes. Minified it is 6,154 bytes, a 41.7 percent reduction, which is the number a minifier will proudly show you. After gzip, the pretty printed version is 668 bytes and the minified version is 599 bytes. The real saving on the wire is 10.3 percent, not 41.7 percent.
minifier_deep_p3: The conclusion is not that minifying is pointless, it is that the payoff depends on where the bytes live. Minify when the size is uncompressed and counted directly: rows in a database column, values in localStorage or Redis, documents you are charged for by the byte, or payloads that must fit a fixed field. For an HTTP response body behind a CDN, enabling compression matters far more than minifying, and doing both buys you about a tenth on top.
minifier_ref_title: Measured sizes for a 40 record array
minifier_ref_intro: The same document at each stage, measured with Node and zlib defaults. Reproduce it yourself before trusting any minification claim, including this one.
minifier_ref_n1: Pretty printed baseline with two space indentation.
minifier_ref_n2: Minified. 41.7 percent smaller than the baseline.
minifier_ref_n3: Baseline after gzip. Compression alone beats minification by a wide margin.
minifier_ref_n4: Minified and gzipped. Only 10.3 percent below the gzipped baseline.
minifier_ex_intro: Whitespace between tokens disappears. Whitespace inside a string value does not.
minifier_ex_note: The two spaces in "New York" survive because they are part of the string. Every other space, newline, and indent is gone.
minifier_pit1_d: Minifying removes redundant characters but leaves the result as plain text that a human can still read. It is not gzip, brotli, or a binary format like MessagePack or CBOR. If you need a genuinely small payload, compress after minifying, and expect compression to do most of the work.
minifier_pit2_t: Newlines inside string values are preserved, and that is correct
minifier_pit2_d: A JSON string containing an escaped newline keeps it, because removing it would change the data. If you expected a multi line string to collapse onto one line, minification is not the tool for that. Rewrite the value itself.
minifier_pit3_d: Running an already minified document through again returns it unchanged and reports zero savings. There is no second pass of redundancy to remove, because whitespace between tokens is the only thing minification touches.
minifier_faq_q6: Is minified JSON still valid JSON?
minifier_faq_a6: Yes. Whitespace between tokens is insignificant in JSON, so removing it produces a document that any conforming parser reads identically. The only cost is readability.
minifier_faq_q7: Does minifying lose precision on large numbers?
minifier_faq_a7: Minifying goes through the same parse and re-serialize cycle as formatting, so integers beyond 2^53 are rounded. That is a property of parsing JSON numbers as doubles, not of minification itself. Send large IDs as strings if this matters.
sorter_deep_title: The sort is locale aware, not byte order
sorter_deep_p1: Keys are compared with the browser locale collation rather than by character code, and the two disagree more often than you would expect. Locale collation treats letters as primary and case as a tiebreaker, so alpha sorts before Beta. Byte order compares code points, where every uppercase ASCII letter comes before every lowercase one, so Beta would sort before alpha. Feed in Beta, alpha, and Alpha and this tool returns alpha, Alpha, Beta.
sorter_deep_p2: Accented and non Latin characters show the difference more sharply. The key école has a code point above z, so byte order would place it after zebra. Locale collation treats it as an e and places it first. If you are producing a canonical form that a program on another platform has to reproduce byte for byte, locale collation is the wrong tool, because the result depends on the collation tables of the environment that produced it.
sorter_deep_p3: Sorting is also not natural sort. The keys item2 and item10 are compared as text, so item10 lands before item2 because the character 1 precedes 2. There is no numeric awareness inside a key name. If you need numbered keys in numeric order, pad them with leading zeros at the source, or restructure the data as an array where position is explicit.
sorter_ref_intro: Each row is a real pair of keys and the order this tool produces in ascending mode, next to what a plain code point comparison would have produced.
sorter_ref_n1: Byte order would give Beta, alpha. Letters outrank case here.
sorter_ref_n2: Same letter, so case decides and lowercase comes first.
sorter_ref_n3: Byte order would give zebra, école. The accent is folded to e.
sorter_ref_n4: Not a natural sort. Compared as text, so 1 precedes 2.
sorter_ref_n5: Underscore sorts before letters in both schemes, so this one agrees.
sorter_ex_intro: Keys are reordered at the top level and inside the nested object. The array keeps its original element order.
sorter_ex_note: The tags array still reads z, a because element order is data. Inside meta, the keys were reordered independently of the parent.
sorter_pit1_t: Numeric keys ignore the sort direction entirely
sorter_pit1_d: Keys made only of digits are stored ahead of every string key in ascending numeric order, and re-serializing cannot override that. Sorting the object with keys b, 10, a, 2 in descending mode returns 2, 10, b, a. The digit keys came out ascending and first, in direct contradiction of the direction you selected. This is a property of the object model, not a bug in the comparison, and no browser based tool can avoid it.
sorter_pit2_t: Sorted output is not a portable canonical form
sorter_pit2_d: Because collation is locale dependent and numeric keys are repositioned, two environments can produce different byte sequences from the same input. Do not hash sorted output and compare it against a hash computed by another implementation. Use a specified canonicalization scheme such as JCS, which mandates code point ordering, if you need that guarantee.
sorter_pit3_t: Sorting before diffing helps, but only for objects
sorter_pit3_d: Sorting removes key order noise from a diff, which is its most common use. It does nothing about array order noise, because arrays are deliberately left alone. If two documents contain the same list in a different sequence, a diff will still report every position as changed.
sorter_faq_q6: Why are my numeric keys not following the sort direction?
sorter_faq_a6: Keys consisting only of digits are held separately from string keys and always emitted in ascending numeric order, before every other key. Descending mode cannot change that. It is a property of how JavaScript objects store keys, so it affects every browser based JSON tool.
sorter_faq_q7: Can I sort array elements too?
sorter_faq_a7: No, and that is deliberate. Array position usually carries meaning, such as ranking or sequence, so reordering elements would change your data rather than normalize its shape. Only object keys are reordered.
diff_deep_title: Arrays are matched by position, and that matters
diff_deep_p1: Objects are matched by key, which is the obvious and correct behaviour. Arrays are matched by index, which is the simple behaviour but not always the one you want. Index matching means element zero is compared to element zero regardless of content, so it reports what changed at each position rather than which items were added or removed.
diff_deep_p2: The consequence shows up when a list is reordered. Take a three element array and move the first item to the end. Nothing was added or removed, but every position now holds a different value, so the diff reports three changes. Insert one item at the front of a ten element array and you get ten reports: nine changed positions and one addition at the tail. The output is accurate about positions, and misleading if you read it as a report about items.
diff_deep_p3: When you care about identity rather than position, sort both arrays by a stable key before comparing, or compare the collections keyed by id instead of as arrays. The JSON Key Sorter handles object keys but deliberately leaves array order alone, so array normalization is something you have to do at the data level. For arrays whose order genuinely is the data, such as a ranking or a sequence of events, index matching is exactly right.
