diff_ref_n1: The path exists only on the right. The value shown is the new one.
diff_ref_n2: The path exists only on the left. The value shown is the one that disappeared.
diff_ref_n3: The path exists on both sides with different values. Old is listed first, then new.
diff_ref_n4: Object keys are joined with dots, at any depth.
diff_ref_n5: Array elements are addressed by index in square brackets.
diff_ref_n6: Used when the two top level values differ in type, such as an object against an array.
diff_ex_title: Comparing two versions of a record
diff_ex_intro: One value changed, one key was removed, and one key was added.
diff_ex_note: The paths are complete, so name and meta.city can be read directly as accessors. Note that no output is produced for keys that are identical on both sides.
diff_pit1_t: Reordering a list looks like a rewrite
diff_pit1_d: Because arrays are matched by index, moving one element reports a change at every position it shifted. A three item list with the head moved to the tail produces three change entries even though the set of items is identical. Sort both sides by a stable field first if you want to compare membership rather than order.
diff_pit2_t: A type change is reported as a single change, not a removal plus an addition
diff_pit2_d: If a path holds the number 1 on the left and the string "1" on the right, or an object on one side and an array on the other, you get one tilde entry showing both values. The comparison does not descend into mismatched types, so you will not see a breakdown of what was inside the object that got replaced.
diff_pit3_t: Identical values short circuit, including identical nulls
diff_pit3_d: Comparison stops as soon as two values are strictly equal, so a key present on both sides with the value null produces no output. If you are hunting for fields that are null when they should be populated, a diff against another document will not surface them. Use the viewer to inspect a single document for that.
diff_faq_q6: Why does reordering an array produce so many differences?
diff_faq_a6: Arrays are compared position by position, so shifting one element changes the value at every position after it. Each of those positions is reported. Sort both arrays by a stable key before comparing if you care about membership rather than order.
diff_faq_q7: Does formatting or key order affect the result?
diff_faq_a7: No. Both sides are parsed before comparison, so indentation, whitespace, and the order of object keys are invisible to the diff. Only the parsed values are compared.
to_typescript_deep_title: What the inference can and cannot know
to_typescript_deep_p1: Optionality is inferred only from arrays. If you paste an array of objects and a key is missing from some elements, that key is marked optional with a question mark. If you paste a single object, every key it has is required and every key it lacks does not exist, because a single sample offers no evidence either way. This is why an array of two or three representative records produces much better types than one object.
to_typescript_deep_p2: A null value produces the type null, not a nullable version of some other type. There is no way to tell from null alone whether the field is a nullable string or a nullable number, so the generator reports exactly what it saw. You almost always want to widen these by hand to string | null or whatever the field really is. The same reasoning applies to an empty array, which becomes any[] because its element type is unobservable.
to_typescript_deep_p3: Nested objects are extracted into their own interfaces named after the key that held them, converted to PascalCase. A key named nested yields interface Nested, and the parent refers to it by name rather than inlining the shape. Two structurally identical objects under different keys therefore produce two interfaces rather than one shared one, so deduplicating them is a manual step if you care about it.
to_typescript_ref_title: How JSON values map to TypeScript types
to_typescript_ref_intro: Every row is a real inference this tool performs. The last three are the ones that need your attention after copying.
to_typescript_ref_n1: Straightforward. All JSON numbers become number, integer or not.
to_typescript_ref_n3: A nested object is lifted into its own interface, named from the key in PascalCase.
to_typescript_ref_n4: A mixed array becomes a union of the element types it observed.
to_typescript_ref_n5: Not a nullable string or number. Widen this by hand once you know the real type.
to_typescript_ref_n6: The element type is unobservable from an empty array, so it falls back to any.
to_typescript_ref_n7: Only arrays reveal optionality. A key missing from some elements gets a question mark.
to_typescript_ex_title: Generating interfaces from an array of records
to_typescript_ex_intro: Two records where the second omits a key. That omission is what makes the field optional.
to_typescript_ex_note: The root interface is always named RootObject, and when the input is an array it describes the shape of one element rather than the array itself. Because nickname is absent from the second record, it is optional. Had you pasted only the first record, it would have been required.
to_typescript_pit1_t: A single sample makes every field required
to_typescript_pit1_d: Optionality is derived by comparing objects within an array. Paste one object and you get an interface where nothing is optional, which will typecheck against your sample and then fail at runtime the first time the API omits a field. Paste an array with at least one sparse record, or add the question marks yourself.
to_typescript_pit2_t: The root interface is called RootObject
to_typescript_pit2_d: The generated name is RootObject, not Root and not something derived from your data. Rename it after copying to match your domain, and remember to update the references from any nested interfaces if you also rename those.
to_typescript_pit3_t: Generated types describe your sample, not the API contract
to_typescript_pit3_d: Inference cannot see fields your sample happened not to include, cannot know that a string field is really an enum of four values, and cannot know that a number is always an integer. If the API publishes an OpenAPI or JSON Schema document, generate from that instead. Use this tool when no schema exists.
to_typescript_faq_q6: Does it deduplicate identical nested shapes?
to_typescript_faq_a6: No. Each nested object gets an interface named after its key, so two structurally identical objects under different keys produce two interfaces. Merge them by hand if you want a single shared type.
to_typescript_faq_q7: Should I use generated types or a schema?
to_typescript_faq_a7: Prefer a schema when one exists. Generating from OpenAPI or JSON Schema captures optionality, enums, formats, and constraints that no sample can reveal. Use this tool when the API has no published schema and a sample response is all you have.
to_yaml_deep_title: Quoting, and why yes is not a boolean here
to_yaml_deep_p1: The best known YAML hazard is the Norway problem. YAML 1.1 defines a generous set of boolean spellings, including yes, no, on, off, y, and n, so a country code list containing NO can silently become a list containing false. YAML 1.2 narrowed booleans to true and false only, but plenty of readers still implement 1.1 behaviour.
to_yaml_deep_p2: This converter emits quoted strings for any value that a looser reader could coerce. The JSON string "yes" comes out as the quoted YAML scalar with quotes intact, and so does "no". The same protection applies to version numbers: the string "1.10" is quoted, because unquoted it would read as the number 1.1 and lose the trailing zero. If you see quotes in the output where you did not expect them, that is the converter defending the value, not adding noise.
to_yaml_deep_p3: Long strings are folded rather than wrapped mid token. Past the 120 character line width, a scalar is written as a folded block using the greater than and minus indicators, which tells a YAML reader to join the wrapped lines back into a single line and strip the trailing newline. It looks unfamiliar but round trips exactly. Anchors and aliases are disabled, so a value repeated in two places is written out twice rather than referenced, which keeps the output readable at the cost of some bytes.
to_yaml_ref_title: How values are written in the output
to_yaml_ref_intro: Each row is a real JSON value and the exact YAML this tool emits for it.
to_yaml_ref_n1: Quoted, so a YAML 1.1 reader cannot turn it into false. This is the Norway problem defence.
to_yaml_ref_n2: Quoted for the same reason. Unquoted yes reads as true in YAML 1.1.
to_yaml_ref_n3: Quoted to protect the trailing zero. Unquoted it would parse as the number 1.1.
to_yaml_ref_n4: An ordinary word needs no quoting and gets none.
to_yaml_ref_n5: A real boolean is written bare, which is how it should read back.
to_yaml_ref_n6: Written as a block sequence, one dash per element, not inline.
to_yaml_ref_n7: An empty array stays in flow style, because there is no element to put on a line.
to_yaml_ref_n8: Folded block scalar past 120 characters. Reads back as one line with no trailing newline.
to_yaml_ex_intro: Note which strings end up quoted and which do not.
to_yaml_ex_note: Only the values that a YAML reader could misread are quoted. Seoul is written bare because no reader would turn it into anything else.
to_yaml_pit1_t: Do not strip the quotes the converter added
to_yaml_pit1_d: Quotes around values like no, yes, off, or 1.10 are load bearing. Removing them to tidy up the file can change a string into a boolean or a version into a truncated number, and the failure often shows up far from the edit. If a quoted scalar looks ugly, leave it ugly.
to_yaml_pit2_t: YAML is a superset, so converting back is not automatic
to_yaml_pit2_d: Every JSON document is valid YAML, but not every YAML document is valid JSON. Anchors, multiple documents in one file, non string keys, and comments have no JSON equivalent. This tool converts one direction only, and a YAML file that uses those features cannot be represented as JSON without restructuring.
to_yaml_pit3_t: Comments cannot survive a round trip through JSON
to_yaml_pit3_d: If you took a commented YAML config, converted it to JSON somewhere, and are now converting back, the comments are already gone. JSON has no comment syntax, so they were dropped at the first conversion. Keep the original YAML if the comments matter.
to_yaml_faq_q6: Why are some strings quoted and others not?
to_yaml_faq_a6: Quoting is applied only where it is needed to preserve the value. A plain word like Seoul cannot be misread, so it is written bare. A word like no could be read as a boolean by a YAML 1.1 parser, so it is quoted. The rule is minimal quoting, not no quoting.
to_yaml_faq_q7: What is the greater than sign in my output?
to_yaml_faq_a7: It is a folded block scalar, used for strings longer than the 120 character line width. The following lines are joined back into one line when read, and the minus suffix strips the trailing newline. The value round trips exactly.
to_csv_deep_title: Quoting rules and the two things Excel will argue with
to_csv_deep_p1: A field is wrapped in double quotes only when it has to be, which is when it contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline. Inside a quoted field, each double quote is doubled, so the value said "hi" becomes the field with doubled inner quotes. Everything else is written bare, which keeps the output readable and diffable rather than uniformly quoted.
to_csv_deep_p2: Two deliberate deviations from RFC 4180 are worth knowing before you hand the file to someone. First, records are separated with a single line feed rather than the carriage return and line feed pair the specification requires. Nearly every tool accepts line feeds, but a strict RFC 4180 parser is entitled to complain. Second, no byte order mark is written. Excel on Windows reads a UTF-8 CSV without a byte order mark using the system code page, which turns non ASCII names into mojibake.
to_csv_deep_p3: Both are easy to work around. If Excel garbles accented or CJK text, import the file through the Data then From Text dialog and select UTF-8 explicitly instead of double clicking it, or prepend a byte order mark with a text editor. Google Sheets and LibreOffice both detect UTF-8 correctly and need neither workaround.
to_csv_ref_title: How each JSON value becomes a cell
to_csv_ref_intro: Each row shows a value inside a record and the exact text this tool writes into the cell.
to_csv_ref_n1: No special characters, so no quoting is added.
to_csv_ref_n2: Quoted because of the comma, which would otherwise split the field.
to_csv_ref_n3: Quoted, and each inner double quote is doubled.
to_csv_ref_n4: Serialized as JSON text, then quoted because that text contains quotes.
to_csv_ref_n5: Arrays get the same treatment. They arrive as a string, not as extra columns.
to_csv_ref_n6: Written as an empty cell. A missing key produces the same result, so the two are indistinguishable.
to_csv_ref_n7: Booleans and numbers are written bare, exactly as they read in JSON.
to_csv_ex_intro: The second record lacks note and meta, and adds tags. Watch where tags lands in the header.
to_csv_ex_note: The header is the union of all keys in first seen order, so tags is last even though it belongs to the second record. Cells for keys a record does not have are empty, and so is the cell for the null score.
to_csv_pit1_t: Empty cell means either null or absent, with no way to tell them apart
to_csv_pit1_d: A key holding null and a key that is missing entirely both produce an empty cell. If that distinction matters in your data, CSV cannot carry it and you need to encode it yourself, for example by substituting a sentinel string before converting. This is a limitation of the format, not of the tool.
to_csv_pit2_t: Nested data becomes a string, not columns
to_csv_pit2_d: An object under a key arrives in one cell as JSON text. It is not flattened into columns like user.city, and a spreadsheet will treat it as an opaque string. If you want real columns, flatten the structure in your own code before converting, or convert the nested arrays separately as their own tables.
to_csv_pit3_t: Excel on Windows may garble non ASCII text
to_csv_pit3_d: The output is UTF-8 with no byte order mark. Double clicking the file on Windows makes Excel guess the system code page, which corrupts accented and CJK characters. Import through the Data then From Text dialog and choose UTF-8, or add a byte order mark first. Sheets and LibreOffice handle it correctly either way.
to_csv_faq_q6: Why does Excel show my Korean or accented text as garbage?
to_csv_faq_a6: The output is UTF-8 without a byte order mark, and Excel on Windows falls back to the system code page when it cannot find one. Import the file through Data then From Text and select UTF-8 rather than double clicking it. Google Sheets and LibreOffice detect the encoding correctly.
to_csv_faq_q7: Does the output use CRLF line endings?
to_csv_faq_a7: No, records are separated by a single line feed. Virtually every spreadsheet and parser accepts this, but a strict RFC 4180 implementation expects a carriage return and line feed pair, so convert the line endings if you are feeding a pedantic consumer.
csv_to_json_deep_title: Every value is a string, and that is the safe choice
csv_to_json_deep_p1: CSV carries no type information at all. The characters 42 in a cell could be the number forty two, a string, a product code, or a truncated identifier, and nothing in the file says which. This converter therefore emits every value as a JSON string, without exception. It is the one behaviour people most often want changed, and the one most likely to corrupt data if it were changed.
csv_to_json_deep_p2: Consider what type guessing costs. A postal code column containing 07030 becomes the number 7030 and the leading zero is gone. A part number like 1E5 becomes 100000 in scientific notation. An identifier of twenty digits gets rounded past the sixteenth. A column of version strings where one row reads 1.10 becomes 1.1. Each of these is a silent, irreversible change to a value that looked like a number but was not one.
csv_to_json_deep_p3: Converting types is far safer once you know what a column means, which is knowledge that lives in your code rather than in the file. Take the string output and map it deliberately, coercing the columns you know are numeric and leaving identifiers alone. It is a few lines of work and it never eats a leading zero.
csv_to_json_ref_title: What the parser does with each input
csv_to_json_ref_intro: Each row is a real CSV fragment and the value this tool produces from it.
csv_to_json_ref_n1: A quoted field keeps its comma. The comma does not split the field.
csv_to_json_ref_n2: A doubled double quote inside a quoted field becomes one literal quote.
csv_to_json_ref_n3: A newline inside quotes stays in the value rather than ending the record.
csv_to_json_ref_n4: A numeric looking field stays a string, so the leading zero survives.
csv_to_json_ref_n5: No type guessing at all, so this stays text rather than becoming 100000.
csv_to_json_ref_n6: A record shorter than the header gets empty strings for the missing fields.
csv_to_json_ref_n7: Carriage return and line feed pairs are handled, so Windows files need no conversion.
csv_to_json_ex_intro: A file with an embedded comma, an escaped quote, and a value that looks like a number.
csv_to_json_ex_note: The zip code kept its leading zero because it stayed a string. Had the parser guessed types, 07030 would have become 7030 and the value would be wrong for every downstream consumer.
csv_to_json_pit1_t: You will need to convert types yourself
csv_to_json_pit1_d: Numbers arrive as strings, so a sum over a column will concatenate instead of adding, and a comparison will order 100 before 20. Map the columns you know are numeric after conversion. Do not reach for a converter that guesses, because it will guess wrong on identifiers and postal codes.
csv_to_json_pit2_t: Only the comma is treated as a delimiter
csv_to_json_pit2_d: Tab separated and semicolon separated files are not parsed. Semicolons are common in exports from European locale spreadsheets, where the comma is the decimal separator. Re-export as comma separated, or replace the delimiter first, being careful not to touch delimiters that appear inside quoted fields.
csv_to_json_pit3_t: A duplicate header name silently wins
csv_to_json_pit3_d: If two columns share a header, both write to the same object key and the rightmost column overwrites the others. JSON objects cannot hold two identical keys, so nothing warns you and one column disappears. Rename the columns in the source before converting.
csv_to_json_faq_q6: Does it handle Windows line endings and multi line fields?
csv_to_json_faq_a6: Yes to both. Carriage return and line feed pairs, lone carriage returns, and lone line feeds all end a record, and a newline inside a quoted field stays part of the value because the whole document is scanned rather than split into lines first.
csv_to_json_faq_q7: What happens if two columns have the same header?
csv_to_json_faq_a7: Both map to the same object key and the rightmost one wins, because a JSON object cannot hold duplicate keys. No warning is shown, so rename the columns in the source file before converting.
to_xml_deep_title: Element names, and the two cases that would otherwise produce invalid XML
to_xml_deep_p1: XML element names are far more restrictive than JSON keys. A JSON key can be any string at all, including an empty one, while an XML name may only contain letters, digits, hyphens, underscores, and periods, and may not begin with a digit or a hyphen. A key like my key or a.b therefore cannot be used directly, and the converter replaces the characters XML rejects with underscores, giving my_key and a_b.
to_xml_deep_p2: Character replacement alone is not enough, because a key such as 2nd survives it unchanged and still cannot start an element name. Such names get an underscore prefix, so 2nd becomes _2nd. This matters because the alternative is output that looks fine, copies cleanly, and then fails at the first parse on the other side, which is a considerably worse outcome than a slightly ugly name.
to_xml_deep_p3: The second invalid case is a top level array. XML permits exactly one root element, so mapping an array of two records straight through would produce two sibling roots and an unparseable document. A top level array is therefore wrapped in a single root element with each entry written as an item element. Arrays nested under a key keep the repeated sibling convention, because there the parent element already provides the required single container.
to_xml_ref_title: How JSON constructs map to XML
to_xml_ref_intro: Each row is a real input fragment and the exact markup this tool emits.
to_xml_ref_n1: An object key becomes an element containing the value.
to_xml_ref_n2: Array items repeat the element name of the key that held them.
to_xml_ref_n3: Null becomes a self closing element. An empty object and an empty array produce the same thing.
to_xml_ref_n4: Ampersand, less than, greater than, and double quote are escaped in text content.
to_xml_ref_n5: Characters XML does not allow in a name become underscores.
to_xml_ref_n6: A name cannot start with a digit, so an underscore is prefixed.
to_xml_ref_n7: A top level array is wrapped, because XML allows only one root element.
to_xml_ex_intro: Note the escaped ampersand, the repeated tags element, and the self closing element for null.
to_xml_ex_note: The apostrophe in a value would be left as is, which is valid in element text content. Only ampersand and less than strictly require escaping there, and this converter also escapes greater than and double quote for safety.
to_xml_pit1_t: Converting back is ambiguous, so the round trip is lossy
to_xml_pit1_d: A single element cannot be distinguished from a one item array, so a tags element appearing once could have come from either. XML also has no number type, so 42 and "42" produce identical markup. Nothing is lost going to XML, but reconstructing the original JSON from that XML requires knowledge the document does not carry, usually a schema.
to_xml_pit2_t: Everything becomes an element, never an attribute
to_xml_pit2_d: If the consumer expects an id as an attribute rather than a child element, this output will not satisfy it. There is no convention in JSON for marking a key as an attribute, so the converter cannot infer the intent. Edit the output by hand for a small document, or use a schema driven serializer for anything larger.
to_xml_pit3_d: SOAP envelopes and most enterprise schemas require namespace declarations and prefixed element names. The output here has neither, so it is a starting point for a request body rather than a finished one. Add the envelope and the namespace attributes after converting.
to_xml_faq_q6: Can I convert the XML back to JSON?
to_xml_faq_a6: Not reliably, and not with this tool. A single element and a one item array produce identical markup, and XML has no number type, so 42 and "42" are indistinguishable. Reconstructing the original JSON needs a schema that says which elements repeat and which are numeric.
to_xml_faq_q7: Why is there no SOAP envelope or namespace?
to_xml_faq_a7: Envelopes and namespaces are specific to the service you are calling, and nothing in your JSON indicates which ones to use. The converter produces a clean document body. Wrap it in the envelope and add the namespace declarations your endpoint requires.
viewer_deep_title: What the tree shows that raw text does not
viewer_deep_p1: Every node is labelled with one of six types: string, number, boolean, null, object, or array. That last distinction is the one raw text handles worst, because arrays and objects are both bracketed and a quick glance at a deeply indented document does not reliably tell you which you are looking at. It matters when you are writing an accessor, since one needs an index and the other needs a key.
viewer_deep_p2: Nodes carry a path built as you would write it in code, with dots for object keys and square brackets for array indices, rooted at root. A field three levels down reads as root.user.address.city, and an element inside an array reads as root.items[2].id. Drop the leading root and you have an expression you can paste into your own code or a jq filter.
viewer_deep_p3: The first two levels are expanded when a document loads and everything deeper starts collapsed. That is a deliberate compromise: expanding everything makes a large response unreadable and slow to render, while collapsing everything means clicking before you can see anything at all. Two levels is usually enough to show the shape of a response and the names of its top level fields.
viewer_ref_intro: What each value in a document is labelled as, and how its path is written.
viewer_ref_n1: Distinct from the number 42, which is the distinction raw text makes easiest to miss.
viewer_ref_n2: A real number. No quotes in the raw text.
viewer_ref_n3: Labelled null rather than being shown as an empty value, so it cannot be mistaken for an empty string.
viewer_ref_n4: An empty string is a string, not a null and not an absent key.
viewer_ref_n5: Arrays and objects are labelled separately, which bracket counting does not do for you.
viewer_ref_n6: Object keys are joined with dots, rooted at root.
viewer_ref_n7: Array elements use bracketed indices, so the path reads as a real accessor.
viewer_ex_title: Reading a response as a tree
viewer_ex_intro: The paths on the right are what the tree reports for each leaf in the document on the left.
viewer_ex_note: Strip the leading root and each path is a valid JavaScript accessor. Note that zip is a string, so its leading zero is intact, while score is a number.
viewer_pit1_t: Very large documents are limited by browser memory
viewer_pit1_d: The whole document is parsed and a tree node is built for every value, which costs several times the size of the raw text in memory. A file of a few megabytes is comfortable. Tens of megabytes will make the tab sluggish or run it out of memory, because nothing is streamed or virtualized. For files that big, work on a slice or use a streaming parser locally.
viewer_pit2_t: Duplicate keys collapse before the tree is built
viewer_pit2_d: If a payload contains the same key twice in one object, parsing keeps only the last occurrence, so the tree shows one node and gives no hint that anything was discarded. This is standard parser behaviour rather than something the viewer chooses. Search the raw text if you suspect a producer is emitting duplicates.
viewer_pit3_t: Large integers are already rounded by the time you see them
viewer_pit3_d: JSON numbers are parsed as double precision floats, so an integer beyond 2^53 loses precision during parsing, before the tree is built. A twenty digit ID will display with trailing zeros that were not in your input. Check the raw editor for the original text, and ask the producer to send such IDs as strings.
viewer_faq_q6: How do I tell a null from an empty string?
viewer_faq_a6: Every node is labelled with its type, so a null reads as null and an empty string reads as a string with no content. In raw text those two look similar enough to confuse while scanning, which is one of the main reasons to use the tree.
viewer_faq_q7: Can I copy the path to a value?
viewer_faq_a7: Each node carries a path written the way you would write it in code, with dots for object keys and bracketed indices for array elements, rooted at root. Drop the leading root and you have an accessor you can paste into your own code.
